Carol Moseley Braun. The first Black woman elected to the United States Senate, representing Illinois from 1993 to 1999. A lawyer and diplomat, she broke two historic barriers simultaneously—gender and race—in one of the upper chamber's most significant electoral breakthroughs.

She was elected in 1992 in a stunning upset against an incumbent Republican senator. Her 1992 election came amid a surge of women's political organizing and backlash against the Clarence Thomas hearings, making her victory a watershed moment. During those confirmation hearings, she served on the Senate Judiciary Committee, where she questioned witnesses on issues of sexual harassment and race.

Braun was a former prosecutor and Illinois state legislator, pioneering a legislative voice centered on civil rights, education, and economic justice. In 2004, she ran for the Democratic presidential nomination, expanding the visible range of Black female political ambition on a national stage. After leaving the Senate, she later served as U.S. Ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa, representing American diplomacy in the Pacific and extending Black political representation into the international sphere.
